stories.title: Public sector union leaders to meet over pay deal row
stories.summary: The leaders of the four largest public sector unions are due to meet to assess the impact of yesterday's strike and to discuss their next steps. A 24-hour work stoppage by more than 300,000 public sector workers concluded at midnight. The action led to widespread disruption throughout the day, including the closure of schools and the cancellation of thousands of hospital appointments. Unions have accused the Government of failing to make meaningful commitments on pay following the expiration of the last public sector pay deal at the end of June. But yesterday evening, Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform Jack Chambers said there was intensive work going on in the background and that he was hopeful a way forward could be found in the coming days. He also said the €1.2 billion for a public sector pay deal announced in the Budget is the "starting point" for discussions and the only way to develop that is to agree to have talks.

stories.title: People 'know' who carried out Waterford attack - gardaí
stories.summary: Gardaí believe there are people in Waterford "who know the person or persons" who carried out an arson attack which killed four people and appealed for them to come forward. Kim English, Philip English and their sons, 12-year-old Callum and nine-year-old Jayden, died after an incendiary device set fire to their home in the Birchwood estate yesterday morning. Two other children, who are aged 14 and six, remain in a critical condition at CHI Crumlin. In a statement, Chief Superintendent Anthony Pettit said gardaí believe the house was attacked deliberately. "There are people in the community who know the person or persons who carried out this arson attack in which four people have been murdered. "If you have any information on the murderous arson attack, please speak to the garda investigation team at Waterford Garda Station or contact the Garda Confidential Line 1800 666 111 or speak with any member of An Garda Síochána that you know," he said.

stories.title: Talks with unions can 'absolutely' begin with pay, says Chambers
stories.summary: Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said that pay can "absolutely" be the starting point for negotiations on a new public sector pay deal, in a move senior union officials said appeared to represent a shift in position. On Monday, in an effort to avert strikes, the Minister wrote to unions proposing that pay be discussed as "a priority alongside other matters," such as reforms or productivity agreements. That position was rejected by unions, who for months have been saying any negotiations on a public service pay agreement "must begin" with "a credible approach to pay." Asked on Prime Time whether pay could be the starting point for negotiations, Minister Chambers replied: "Absolutely," and repeated the position when asked to clarify. "We're obviously going to face a strike now tomorrow," he told presenter Miriam O'Callaghan, "and my work in the days to come is to put this into a process of constructive, meaningful engagement and to get a fair and substantial negotiated outcome for public sector workers and something that's sustainable and affordable for the state as well." "With pay as a starting point?" asked Ms O'Callaghan, to which Minister Chambers replied, "Absolutely. That's being put out there as a deflective mechanism to actually continue this escalation."

stories.title: Anthropic pre-IPO meeting hears of surging revenue
stories.summary: Anthropic has told prospective investors that revenue in the third quarter surged 45% from the prior quarter, two people who attended an investor day said, a move that could assuage market concerns about the huge costs of developing AI systems. Third-quarter revenue rose to $16.8 billion from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first quarter, the people said. Anthropic told the group the company was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter, they added. The meeting in San Francisco was meant to familiarise prospective Anthropic investors with the company before its highly anticipated IPO. The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI, making Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for loss-making AI developers investing heavily to pursue massive scale. Its public-market debut is likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections, Reuters has reported. Attendees at yesterday's event met with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and came away optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability, a few of them told Reuters as they left its headquarters in the evening.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said that "massive" ⁠oil, gas and mineral exploration is getting ready to begin in Greenland. He did not share details about the exploration plans in Greenland but said, "there are experts that are saying that the amount of easily available oil is far greater ‌than that ⁠of almost any land, anywhere in the world." The United States, Denmark and Greenland last month signed an agreement, aimed at ending tensions after Mr Trump's repeated threats to take control ‌of the strategically located and mineral-rich island. "Any future attack on the ⁠United States will have to come across ‌Greenland, where our defence will routinely knock down drones, ⁠missiles, ‌or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," Mr Trump added in his post on Truth Social. The ⁠deal signed between the US, Denmark and Greenland expands ⁠the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Mr Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. stories.title: Murphy's star keeps rising as Aviva dream within grasp
stories.summary: Emily Murphy has enjoyed a very good year with the Republic of Ireland. The 23-year-old made her debut against Wales in March 2024, during Eileen Gleeson's time in charge. There was instant excitement about the former Chelsea academy talent who had represented England at underage level (her dad is a Dubliner, TV personality Baz Ashmawy is her godfather). Murphy was playing her football at Wake Forest University in America for the first year of her international career but a move to Newcastle United in WSL2, just before Carla Ward took the reins, helped her go to another level. Brighton and Hove Albion won the race to bring Murphy to the WSL last summer, and she has matured into a consistently productive creative outlet for her country. There will be loads of talk about star attacker Ewa Pajor in the build-up to the Republic of Ireland's World Cup play-off final against Poland in six weeks' time. But nobody should sleep on Murphy, the fleet-footed forward with an appetite for graft.

stories.title: Two-time All-Ireland winner Morley calls time on Kerry
stories.summary: Kerry's two-time All-Ireland winner Tadhg Morley has announced his retirement from inter-county football. The 33-year-old defender enjoyed 11 seasons with the Kingdom, with the Sam Maguire successes of 2022 and 2025 the high points in a career that also yielded 10 Munster titles, five Division One league titles and an All-Star in 2022. The Templenoe man was handed his debut under Éamonn Fitzmaurice in 2016 and would go on to establish himself in the Kerry rearguard under Peter Keane and Jack O’Connor. The majority of his 57 championship appearances came in the half-back line where he normally anchored the defence, but often slotted into the number 3 jersey when required. His final appearance in the Green and Gold came off the bench in this year's quarter-final victory over Tyrone. "After many proud and unforgettable years, I’ve decided the time has come to bring my Kerry football journey to an end," he said in a statement today.

stories.title: Ireland finish Kazakhstan rout to set up Poland showdown
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland's World Cup mission has been crystallised after they sauntered past Kazakhstan at SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh to reach the play-off final. If they beat Poland over two legs in late November/early December, the Girls in Green are going to Brazil. That will not be straightforward. After Friday's 8-0 win in the first leg, this clash in Cork was effectively a dead-rubber. Jessie Stapleton, Katie McCabe, Lucy Quinn and Denise O'Sullivan got the goals in a game that often resembled a training session. The real drama was in Gdansk. The Poles – inspired by brilliant Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor – defeated Belgium on penalties in the other semi-final, which had ended 3-3 on aggregate. Last April, Ireland beat Poland twice in a World Cup qualification double-header: 3-2 in Gdansk, and 1-0 in Dublin. But be warned: during League A qualification for Euro 2025, Poland lost twice to Austria, only to prevail 2-0 on aggregate when the countries later collided in the play-offs. They have form when it comes to peaking at the right time. The play-off final will be a nerve-shredder, but tonight, there was no jeopardy. Ireland completed the formalities without breaking a sweat.

stories.title: Lions women to start tour with Cardiff game versus France
stories.summary: The British & Irish women's squad will kickstart their 2027 tour schedule on home soil, facing France in Cardiff on Friday, 27 August. Dubbed 'The Howden Lions Women's Cup', the fixture will be the first opportunity to watch Jo Yapp’s side in action before heading to New Zealand. The tour begins on Saturday, 4 September when the Lions women face a Black Ferns XV at Semenoff Stadium in Whangarei, before the historic first test against the Black Ferns at Go Media Stadium in Auckland on Saturday, 11 September. The Lions will then take on an Invitational XV at FMG Stadium Waikato in Hamilton on 14 September, before the second test in Wellington on Saturday, 18 September. The series concludes with the third and final test at One NZ Stadium in Christchurch on 25 September. Speaking at the fixture announcement, British & Irish Lions women’s head coach Yapp said of the fixture announcement: "There are moments in sport that only come around once - and this is one of them.

stories.title: On the Air - the early days of arts programming on RTÉ
stories.summary: We present an extract from On the Air – 100 Years of Irish Radio, the new book by Rosemary Day. For 100 years, radio has been the voice of the nation, bringing us together and reflecting our changing society. As the only broadcast medium in Irish households for much of the twentieth century, Radio Éireann had a responsibility to entertain – you could nearly say they had a captive audience – and they took this responsibility seriously, with drama outweighing variety shows right up to the 1970s. Radio didn’t know how to do drama at the outset and began by transferring plays written for the stage directly onto the air, with theatre actors delivering lines at great volume, sometimes dressed in full costume. Broadcasters realised that this needed some adaptation; the BBC commissioned its first play specifically for the medium in its very first year. The playwright Richard Ash struggled with the nature of the blind medium. How was he to portray anything when the listener could see nothing? He solved the problem by setting Danger! in a mine and the first line was ‘The lights have gone out!’ It didn’t take long for writers, actors and producers to realise that the pictures we make in our minds are powerful images, possibly even more powerful than those we see. A new art form was born, and Radio Éireann, despite its limited finances, invested in scripts and actors, delivering hundreds of plays a year to Irish audiences, including at least one a week in Irish. The nature of theatre work made it difficult to know who would be available and when for any production. This meant radio drama was stressful for all involved. In 1946, the Radio Éireann Players (REP) were formed, making things far easier to manage. This small band of actors performed in almost everything that went out on air, and not just drama: they were called on to read scripts for every talk programme the station produced. They had to be bilingual and able to take on multiple roles and personas. They worked hard, with rehearsals or read-throughs each morning, and performances, live in front of the microphone, each afternoon or evening. But it was a better life for most, or at least a more secure one, in terms of pay and conditions, than the theatre. The REP appear to have been a close knit group and recall their experiences fondly. Some stayed with the REP all their working lives and others branched out into film, into presentation on radio and television and other fields, for example Niall Tóibín, Eamon Kelly and Breandán Ó Dúill. stories.title: Irish makeup artist Ben Sun on working the Fashion Month circuit
stories.summary: Charlotte Ryan speaks to Ben Sun, an Irish makeup artist who has worked on some of fashion's most talked-about runway shows this season, including McQueen and Irish couture brand Standing Ground, about life behind the scenes of fashion's busiest month. When I speak to Ben Sun, it's mere days after the last show of Paris Fashion Week, which comes at the end of Fashion Month - the four-week stretch of runway shows and events that span across New York, London, Milan and Paris - and he's making chicken soup. Listening to the young makeup artist recount the hectic schedules of the previous 10 days, ping-ponging back and forth from city to city, show to show, it sounds like the soup is doing a lot of spiritual heavy lifting. "I've had only like, two mental breakdowns this week, which is like not the usual five, so I can say it went well", he tells me. "I'm not kidding; I've only cried twice, so it's not as bad as usual." Speaking about the chaotic period, which takes place twice a year, Sun paints a picture of extreme hustle and glamour that certainly lives up to its reputation as the busiest time in fashion: "Paris is where all the magic happens. It's, in my opinion, the biggest and most important fashion week, and it's the one where the most people probably attend, just come to the city. "In the fashion industry, everyone is very connected, and it's all about making those right connections and making sure you're in the right room. So no matter how exhausted you are after shows or during clients, I always try to allow myself to have the energy for a dinner or like an event just to get to know the industry a little bit better. So that's the exhausting part for me."

stories.title: Cases halted as Criminal Courts of Justice staff picket
stories.summary: The Criminal Courts of Justice (CCJ) on Dublin's Parkgate Street was at a standstill as staff mounted a picket on the steps, bringing scheduled legal proceedings to a halt. Court workers and administrative staff gathered at the main entrance to demand a new public pay agreement after the previous national deal expired earlier this year. With workers standing firm on the steps, the doors to the country's main criminal court complex - which houses the Circuit Court, District Court, and Central Criminal Court - remained effectively closed. Court sittings around the country were cancelled, with the exception of emergency domestic violence and childcare applications, Garda applications to remand an accused person in custody where station bail has not been granted, and, in the High Court, injunctions to protect life, health, safety or welfare. Pasted directly onto the CCJ's glass doors behind the picketing staff was an official "Notice of Adjournment of Court" sign. The document notified defendants and members of the public who turned up expecting their cases to be heard that the court clerk had formally adjourned all sittings by order of a District Court judge.

stories.title: NetZero eyes €400m revenue by 2030, workforce to double
stories.summary: NetZero Group, which provides building decarbonisation services, is targeting revenue of €400m by 2030 and the doubling of its workforce as Ireland's home energy upgrade market enters a new phase of growth. This comes on the back of stronger government supports, rising homeowner demand and the urgent need to accelerate the national retrofit programme. NetZero Group, which was formed by Waterland Ireland in 2023, said today it is targeting revenue growth from over €200m today to €400m by 2030. The company provides design, installation, commissioning and lifecycle servicing across heat pumps, solar PV, insulation, ventilation and wider building-decarbonisation solutions. It operates as a fully integrated national platform across three divisions - New Build, Retrofit and Service. The group has installed about 7,300 heat pumps over the past 12 months, with the majority delivered in new-build homes. It has also completed around 3,400 retrofit projects over the past year. The company has over 1,000 employees and subcontractors across 14 locations around the country and said today it plans to double its workforce and contractor network to over 2,000 people by 2030.

stories.summary: Heavy overnight Russian strikes killed at least six people in Ukraine and left hundreds of thousands without power, authorities said, in an attack President Volodymyr Zelensky ⁠called "ostentatious disrespect" to US President Donald Trump's peace effort. The hours-long missile and drone attack primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, and damaged 30 energy facilities, Mr Zelensky said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, he added. Mr Trump, who lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week in a bid to lower politically sensitive fuel prices, has said that both sides agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, though neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed it. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has ‌never before shown such ⁠ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Mr Zelensky wrote on X. "Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong." Russia's defence ministry said it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.

stories.title: Maresca insists City deserved something from PSG thriller
stories.summary: Enzo Maresca believes Manchester City deserved to get something out of a wild 4-2 Champions League loss to Paris St Germain after fighting back from 3-0 down in a chaotic second half. In their first home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules, and with former manager Pep Guardiola watching on, City lost for the first time since the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal in August, a run of eight games. PSG ripped them apart in the first half, storming ahead through quickfire goals from Desire Doue and Ousmane Dembele, then all but killing it when Vitinha made it 3-0 with 32 minutes gone. A triple change at the break helped rouse City as Erling Haaland scored twice, becoming City's record goalscorer in the Champions League in the process as he moved to 38 goals from 41 appearances, while also hitting the crossbar and seeing Enzo Fernandez denied by the post. But in between Haaland’s strikes, Maghnes Akliouche scored PSG’s fourth, the ball squeezing past a despairing Gianluigi Donnarumma, and a comeback proved beyond Maresca’s men even if former City man Ferran Torres missed a late penalty for the visitors. "(It) has been a bit of a strange game, especially because we concede two goals in two minutes that create some problems for us," Maresca said. "Before the first goal we didn’t concede nothing, we had some good moments then after two minutes, we concede the second one so it becomes more difficult.

stories.title: Eight counties represented in Champion 15 hurling team
stories.summary: An eight-county spread of players who featured in the Christy Ring, Nickey Rackard and Lory Meagher Cup competitions makes up the 2026 Champion 15 hurling team of the year. Christy Ring Cup champions Derry are represented by goalkeeper Seán Kelly, defenders Patrick Turner and Conor Coyle, midfield engine Cormac O'Doherty and forwards Deaglán Foley and Shea Cassidy. New York’s second straight piece of silverware after adding the Nickey Rackard to the Meagher Cup won in 2025 is recognised with spots for the rampaging forward AJ Willis and defender and former Tipp footballer Bill Maher. Meanwhile 2026 Lory Meagher Cup winning captain Reuben Murray represents Longford alongside full-back colleague Seán Lancaster. Prolific Kerry forward Padraig Boyle is full-forward, while Sligo’s Andrew Kilcullen and Mayo’s Cormac Philips are other forwards who have had their lasting impact reflected on the team. Joe Murray’s defiance in defence for Leitrim earns him a place in the full-back line and Tyrone’s stylish Fionn Devlin completes the half-back line. The Champion 15 team, who will be honoured at Croke Park on Friday evening, was selected by an independent panel of Gaelic Games correspondents with nominations submitted by GPA player representatives.

stories.title: McCabe: 'If there's a game to come to, it's this one'
stories.summary: Katie McCabe says that securing qualification for another World Cup is her main footballing priority and appealed for a big crowd to descend on Aviva Stadium for the pivotal second leg against Poland in December. McCabe drilled home the second goal on the night as Carla Ward's side completed their business against a weak Kazakhstan outfit, who did at least provide more resistance than they had in Astana last Friday. There were some predictions of double-digit margins after the 8-0 win in the away leg but the Cork crowd had to content themselves with a four, with Jessie Stapleton, Lucy Quinn and local hero Denise O'Sullivan accounting for the others. More significant was the news that Poland had dumped out Belgium on penalties in Gdansk. Ireland have already beaten Poland twice in 2026, a 3-2 win in Gdansk and a 1-0 victory in Aviva Stadium, both coming in the space of a week in April. Now, the Poles are all that stand in the way of a successive World Cup appearance for Ireland. "I think for us, obviously for both teams [Poland and Belgium], we played them very recently, but they're going to be a different team come six weeks, so we need to be ready.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Ezra Williams' cultural picks
stories.summary: Ezra Williams is a Cork-based songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and producer. Their debut album Supernumeraries was nominated for the RTE Choice Music Prize, while their single My Own Person featured in Netflix drama Heartstopper. Catchy but subtle; self-deprecating but never sombre (and always utterly charming) their songs offer an often overlooked take on emotional relationships, with Ezra writing as a person who is non-binary and on the autism spectrum. They are currently working on new music for their next album. Ahead of their appearance at this year's Cork Jazz Festival, we asked Ezra for their choice cultural picks... I love the film Magnolia mainly for the soundtrack by Aimee Mann and I also love the movie Benjamin by Simon Amstell, again because of the soundtrack but also they’re both just very good movies. I usually rewatch films that have a good soundtrack, and I watch most films at home because I like being in bed when I watch a movie. Ive recently been listening to a lot of Lisa O’Neill, Remi Wolf, Stevie Wonder and Frog. Growing up, my main inspirations were Daniel Johnston, Elliott Smith and Kate Bush. In terms of genres, I listen to everything but recently I’ve been leaning more towards folk/trad music and country gaze. I try to go to as many gigs as possible. I don’t read books that much because of my dyslexia, so most of the books that I own are pattern books for knitting - I’m trying to teach myself lace patterns using a 280 Japanese lace stitches book. I’ve tried listening to audio books before, but I can never focus on them, I find it difficult to even take phone calls - I need visuals when taking in information, I think.

stories.title: Blondie to release first album in nine years
stories.summary: New wave band Blondie will release their first album in nine years, featuring the final recording of drummer Clem Burke. The new record, entitled High Noon, will be released in February 2027 and will feature contributions from Johnny Marr, Glen Matlock, Zach Condon of Beirut, Lucius and others. Fronted by singer Debbie Harry, the band has also released the first single from the record, Spectral Eyes, which is out now and was written by Marr, who contributed guitar. The band's 12th studio album marks the final recording of drummer Burke, who died in April 2025 at the age of 70 after a cancer diagnosis. The drummer performed on classic tracks such as Call Me, Heart of Glass and One Way or Another. Harry said: "This album is classic Blondie – an amalgamation of all our different influences and eras into something new.

stories.title: I tried Sauna Aufguss - a steamy, semi-nude wellness experience
stories.summary: Sitting shyly in my grey towel, I feel like the odd one out among a group of mostly naked German and Austrian sauna-goers. Austrian rock music blares as our "sauna masters", dressed in themed outfits, dance around the room, dramatically twirling their towels to fan waves of hot steam towards our faces. The air fills with the delicious scents of orange and rosemary as oil-infused ice sizzles on the hot sauna rocks, releasing fragrant clouds of heat. This is my first Sauna Aufguss experience: a guided, multisensory sauna ritual whose name derives from the German word for "infusion" or "pouring". Rooted in German-speaking sauna culture, the practice is gaining popularity at spas across Europe. An Aufguss session typically lasts 10 to 15 minutes and unfolds in three rounds, during which the sauna masters place balls of flavoured ice on the hot rocks before using elaborate towel movements to circulate the fragrant, humid heat around the room. Our sauna masters, Janine Kavallar and Andi Gyurcsik, are a couple who radiate fun and positive energy. They host these sessions three times a day at Hotel Lürzerhof, an alpine resort just outside Salzburg, where I spend a few days indulging in some much-needed relaxation and outdoor adventure.

stories.title: Universities warn funding gap leaves sector at cliff-edge
stories.summary: Universities are to tell an Oireachtas committee that they are at capacity and teetering on a cliff-edge unless the Government addresses a funding gap in higher education. The head of the Irish Universities Association (IUA), which represents seven universities, will be joined by representatives of Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin and University College Cork, at the Oireachtas Committee on Further and Higher Education later today. The group had sought €190m in additional core funding in Budget 2027 but €10m in additional funding was ultimately provided in last week's announcement. IUA Director General Paul Johnston will tell TDs and Senators how third-level education is underfunded by €250m annually. In 2022, a Government commissioned report identified a €307m funding gap at third-level. "Five budgets later, the original deficit is down to around €130m. But as we know in our own lives, household costs don't stand still as you pay down your mortgage. Unfunded pay costs and unfunded growth in student numbers have pushed the real gap above €250m per annum", Mr Johnston will state in his opening address.

stories.title: Why is the property market cooling down?
stories.summary: This time two years ago property prices were accelerating at a breakneck speed of 10% annually, but the rate of increase has now slowed to 5%. Prices are still rising and there is no sign of them falling at present. Instead, the Irish property market appears to be transitioning to a period of more moderate growth. Chief Economist at Bank of Ireland Conall Mac Coille said: "We are looking at house price inflation of 3% to 4%." He calls it a "chink of light" for people hoping to buy a home. Prices have been steadily rising since 2013 when the market reached rock bottom after the financial crisis.

stories.title: Will lower Dublin Airport passenger charges make flying cheaper?
stories.summary: Analysis: Cheaper airports attract more flights and more seats can push prices down, but surging fuel prices may scupper that Most of us never think about the airport passenger charge when booking a flight. It's levied on the airline, not on you, and how much of it ends up in your fare is the airline's call. Later this year the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) will set the maximum Dublin Airport can charge per passenger for the next five years, and the draft decision has the airport and its biggest customer pulling in opposite directions. The draft determination sets a price cap of €8.85 per passenger for 2027, which is 15% below this year's €10.39. The IAA says that brings the figure back to the €8.46 to €9.54 range of 2023 to 2025. The DAA had asked for an average of €12.86 over the period, rising to €14.99 by 2031. Dublin is the only airport in the State with regulated charges, so Cork, Shannon and the others aren't affected. Submissions closed in September and a final decision is due before the end of the year, so time is short. Not automatically. The cut works out at €1.54 a head, hardly an life-changing amount, and nothing obliges an airline to pass it on. The case for lower fares is indirect: cheaper airports attract more flights, and more seats on a route can push prices down. That's the argument Ryanair is making. It says it will add two million seats at Dublin next summer if the final rates are competitive, and it has tied its 10% Dublin schedule cut this summer to rising charges. It has also said it would base three more aircraft here, making Dublin the first airport to receive its new Boeing 737 MAX-10. Aer Lingus, meanwhile, described the proposed levels as "directionally reasonable" while asking for stronger guarantees that the airport delivers its projects efficiently. There's a catch. The DAA has told the regulator that airlines are already trimming flights because of surging fuel prices and economic uncertainty. A €1.54 saving can easily be swamped by the price of jet fuel.

stories.title: Tributes paid to man killed by tiger at UK wildlife park
stories.summary: The family of William Chapman, who was killed by a tiger at a wildlife park, have described the 23-year-old as a "bright, warm and engaging young man". Mr Chapman, who was killed when he entered the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster on Saturday, had suffered from "significant mental illness over a number of years", his family added in a statement. "The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," they said. The statement urged people to stop sharing video footage of the incident. "The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time," they said. "The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did," the statement added.

stories.title: McIlroy and McKibbin well placed on opening day in India
stories.summary: Tom McKibbin and Rory McIlroy enjoyed fast starts on day one of the DP World India Championship. With play suspended shortly after 11am local time due to lightning, McKibbin shared the lead at five-under-par with McIlroy three shots back. Shane Lowry, who is also teeing it up, is back at one-over-par. It was an impressive opening 16 holes from McKibbin prior to being called off course. The 23-year-old carded six birdies and just the one bogey, with a look at another birdie on the par-five eighth hole, his 17th, upon resumption. McIlroy made bogey on his opening hole, the tenth, but bounced back with birdies on the 13th, 15th, 18th and second holes before dropping another shot on the third hole, his 12th of the day, to sit at two-under-par when play was suspended. Lowry also made a slow start with bogeys on his second and third holes of the day before making the turn in two-over. He did rally with birdies on his tenth and 12th holes of the day before another bogey on the par-three seventh, his 16th, left him back at one-over with two holes still to be played.
